chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
title: Blues guitarists converge on Paducah and the Decca rhythm section date
summary: Jones describes recapitulating the blues for the Decca rhythm section recordings, and where guitarists and banjo players gathered in the South.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: You can play these, as when we did the rhythm section things at Decca Recording. We just sat down to do

these recordings and we had to recapitulate. In other words we had to do a track - in other words we had to figure out from the Joe Pullam days or from whoever, but fortunately for me that I had had to gone through the things and I knew the guitar players. I knew the blues singers. I knew the banjo players, see, because Paducah, Kentucky, introduced to the world - we don't know how it happened but all of the best banjo players and guitar players converged into an area of Kentucky. I know all of the greatest guitarists from Tampa Red or anybody that you ever read about in this thing, I don't care who it was - they came through when they built the Muscle Shoals in Alabama - Florence, Sheffield, and Tuscumbia, coming down through the levee. They converged because that was the only place where they had to go to make a living. We didn't have the recording wherewith because you only had a place where you had to go into St. Louis to make the recordings. Because I go to Lonny Johnson in 1923 with Victoria Spivey and "Furniture Man Blues" but he was a recording artist and there was very difficult in those particular times to have artists to make the people on the things.
There's somebody else by the name of Lonny.
